title: The hidden power
hookLine: sages ask what caused the world, then sit down to meditate, and see a power hidden in plain sight
carry: god's power hides in the world; stillness sees it

lines: THE USUAL ANSWERS DON'T SETTLE IT.
cards: What is the cause? Where did we come from? By what do we live?
Where do we rest? Those are the questions that open the Shvetashvatara Upanishad. A group of seekers run through the usual answers: time, nature, chance, the elements.
None of them settles it. So they turn from the list. They sit, and they meditate.
And the next verse says what they saw. Not a new theory. A power, hidden.

teach.b: Here is the verse, in paraphrase.

teach.h: GOD'S OWN POWER, HIDDEN IN ITS QUALITIES.
teach.b: Those who followed the path of meditation saw the power of God's own self, hidden in its own qualities. The Sanskrit is devatma shakti: the shakti of the divine self. Notice three things.
First, it's seen in meditation, not argued into. The list ran out, they sat, and then they saw. Second, the power is hidden in a surprising place: in its own qualities.

The power behind the world is covered by the world it makes, the way a person can be hidden by their own good work. You see the painting and forget the painter's hand. Third, the power belongs to God's own self.

It isn't a second thing standing beside God. Later the same Upanishad comes back to it. His highest power, the text says, is heard of as many-sided, and his knowledge, strength and action belong to his nature.
Knowing, strength, doing: shakti is the name for God in action.
One more line draws the map.
Know that maya is prakriti, nature, and that the great Lord is the one who wields maya.
Teachers read the word maya there in more than one way, but the shape of the verse is plain: the power that makes nature is in the Lord's hand.
In this Upanishad, the power that makes the world is God's own, folded so deeply into what we see that it takes stillness to notice it.
That's why dhyana, meditation, sits beside prayer in Hindu practice: not to invent the divine, but to see it.

how: The Shvetashvatara Upanishad is read and chanted in Vedanta and Shaiva study, and its verse on God's hidden power is quoted by teachers explaining the idea of shakti.

games.q: you're one of the seekers. time, nature, chance: none of the answers settles where the world comes from. what do you do?
o: keep listing answers until one fits.
decide the question can't be asked.
games.why: they turn to meditation, and the next verse says what they saw: God's own power, hidden in its own qualities.

practice: Many Hindus sit each morning, before the day's noise, in dhyana. Sit now and look at one ordinary thing near you: a plant, your hand, the light on a wall. Don't explain it.
Let the answers pass, the way the seekers let their list go, and keep looking for the power hidden in it. If you pray, rest in the name you use for God; if you don't, rest in the looking.
